title: Food Log Export Kit
user: A calorie tracker user who needs to get years of meals, recipes, and nutrition entries out of a failing or paywalled app into a usable local archive.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN user says Yazio's recipe sharing bug blocks a feature used daily and asks for a replacement calorie counter after losing roughly 30 lb.
A FoodYou user reports its backup/export is always 0 KB and explicitly needs a nonempty export that can be converted to CSV.

recurrence: Two independent 2025–26 requests in consumer tracker and open-source tracker communities; data loss or inability to leave an app is high-severity because the history is personally valuable.
current_workaround: Screenshots, manual CSV transcription, keeping the old app installed, or hoping a proprietary export works.
incumbents_and_gap: Yazio, MyFitnessPal, Cronometer, and FoodYou each own their own export format; generic CSV tools do not recover a readable food/recipe timeline from imperfect exports.
smallest_useful_product: Local desktop/PWA importer for a small, documented set of user-provided exports that validates files, normalizes meals/recipes/weights, flags lossy fields, and writes CSV plus a portable JSON archive. Non-goals: bank-login-style account scraping, calorie recommendations, or cloud sync.
success_measure: At least 80% of supported sample exports finish with no unexplained dropped rows, and 50% of pilot users open the resulting archive again within 30 days.
monetization: one-time — migration is episodic, and a local purchase fits users trying to escape recurring app fees.
constraints: All conversion happens on-device; never collect health or diet data; clearly mark unsupported fields and avoid medical or nutritional advice; use only user-exported files.
why_distinct: It is an exit and preservation utility, not another calorie counter.

title: Calorie Week View
user: Someone logging food who needs a calm weekly view of calories and weight rather than a streak-driven daily dashboard.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN poster new to calorie tracking asks for a balance of reasonable accuracy and flexibility, including eating out, rather than simply choosing an app.
A FoodYou feature request asks for weight progress and a weekly calorie average/chart because daily targets alone do not fit users' goals.

recurrence: Two separate asks spanning 15 months; the recurring need is interpretation over a week, not more database coverage.
current_workaround: Mentally average daily totals, export to a spreadsheet, or accept opaque in-app progress scores.
incumbents_and_gap: MyFitnessPal, Yazio, Cronometer, and FoodYou log food well but center daily targets, subscriptions, social features, or proprietary data stores; a no-account weekly review is not their core artifact.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA accepting manual entries or CSV, showing seven-day calorie/macro bands, optional weight trend, missing-day annotation, and print/export. Non-goals: barcode database, photo estimation, social feeds, coaching, or dieting prescriptions.
success_measure: In a four-week pilot, 70% of users complete at least three weekly reviews and can correctly identify whether their average landed inside their chosen range.
monetization: free — a transparent local calculator earns trust and can spread through CSV compatibility.
constraints: No diagnosis, eating-disorder guidance, or automatic targets; store data in the browser by default and make deletion/export obvious.
why_distinct: The product is a weekly reflection surface for existing logs, not a gamified food-tracking clone.

title: Set Note Progression
user: A recreational lifter who needs to retain the reason behind each set and apply a repeatable double-progression rule next session.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Wger user asks for per-set notes such as 'grip slipped,' 'paused reps,' and 'felt easy, increase next time' because session-level notes are insufficient.
A separate Wger request describes double progression as common hypertrophy practice and asks to increase weight only after every set reaches the top of the rep range.

recurrence: Two distinct detailed fitness-log requests in one active project within a month; missed context produces unsafe or unhelpful weight recommendations.
current_workaround: Put cryptic annotations in a session note, use a spreadsheet, or decide increases from memory.
incumbents_and_gap: Strong, Hevy, Fitbod, and Wger record sets, but generic history views do not make set-level context and one explicit progression gate the next-action surface.
smallest_useful_product: Offline workout log with an exercise template, per-set text chips, rep ranges, and a deterministic 'hold/add reps/increase' suggestion that always exposes its rule. Non-goals: generated workouts, social leaderboards, wearables, or medical injury advice.
success_measure: After 20 logged sessions, 70% of pilot lifters report the suggested next load agrees with their own written set notes in at least 8 of 10 cases.
monetization: one-time — serious personal logs should remain usable without an ongoing account fee.
constraints: No training or medical guarantees; local encrypted export; accessible large tap targets for in-gym use.
why_distinct: It makes the explanation for progression first-class instead of competing as a general workout-plan generator.

title: Health Data Bridge
user: An Android fitness/nutrition logger who needs a visible, local import map from Health Connect data to a personal log without surrendering the full history to another SaaS.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Wger's health-sync umbrella issue proposes reading measurements from Google/Apple health APIs and importing them into the application.
A FoodYou user asks for Health Connect burned-calorie access so daily goals can account for activity.

recurrence: Two independent health-log projects request the same integration boundary; users want their activity and nutrition data to meet without manually reconciling it.
current_workaround: Re-enter activity calories, allow a vendor app broad sync access, or omit activity entirely.
incumbents_and_gap: Health Connect provides the platform store and Google Fit/health apps visualize it; tracker apps add one-off integrations, but users lack a local, inspectable field mapping and import ledger.
smallest_useful_product: Android app that asks for narrow Health Connect read permissions, previews each record type and date range, maps activity/weight records to a local CSV/JSON log, and records idempotent import receipts. Non-goals: cloud backup, calorie prescriptions, Apple Health support in v1, or sharing data with providers.
success_measure: A pilot user imports one month of activity and weight in under five minutes, with zero duplicate records after a second import.
monetization: one-time — the value is a trusted local interoperability utility, not a recurring wellness service.
constraints: Use Android Health Connect permissions only; minimum necessary scopes; no medical claims; encrypt local files; publish a plain-language data-flow screen.
why_distinct: It is an auditable connector and receipt book, not a health dashboard or AI coach.

title: Flex Meal Templates
user: A person reusing meals while changing portion sizes who needs each meal template to remain editable at logging time and fit a meal-specific nutrition budget.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Wger user says fixed ingredient weights in saved meals cannot be adjusted while logging and asks for meals to behave like editable ingredient templates.
A FoodYou request asks for configurable calorie and macro distributions by meal, calculated from daily targets.

recurrence: Two different personal-log products receive adjacent requests in summer 2026: repeat meals are useful only when portions and meal allocations remain flexible.
current_workaround: Duplicate a meal, edit ingredients from scratch, or maintain a separate spreadsheet of portions and macro targets.
incumbents_and_gap: Cronometer, MyFitnessPal, FoodYou, and Wger save meals, but saved meals tend to become rigid entries rather than parameterized personal templates with visible portion deltas.
smallest_useful_product: Offline template editor for 10–30 recurring meals: base ingredients, adjustable serving multiplier, substitutions, per-meal calorie/macro bands, and CSV export. Non-goals: food search, barcode lookup, recipe scraping, or meal-plan generation.
success_measure: At least 60% of pilot users log a reused meal with an adjusted portion at least twice per week, without creating a duplicate template.
monetization: free — a focused local companion should interoperate through import/export before any paid tier is considered.
constraints: Nutrition values are user-entered estimates; no health claims; browser-local storage with export and irreversible-delete controls.
why_distinct: It solves the template-versus-real-portion gap instead of attempting to replace a full nutrition database.

title: Recipe Import Repair
user: A self-hosted recipe keeper moving recipes between formats who needs a deterministic way to inspect and repair broken ingredient/step imports before committing them.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A FoodYou user requests recipe import from structured text such as JSON or Markdown so recipes can be brought in rather than retyped.
A Tandoor user importing from Mealie receives an opaque ingredient parsing error and specifically asks the importer to give a useful hint.

recurrence: Two projects expose the same friction: importing recipes is common, but parse failures are unexplained and leave users with no safe repair path.
current_workaround: Retry imports blindly, hand-edit JSON, retype recipes, or depend on an LLM to rewrite source text.
incumbents_and_gap: Mealie, Tandoor, Paprika, and FoodYou import some formats; their importers are application-specific and error messages do not provide a portable correction workflow.
smallest_useful_product: Local web tool that accepts Recipe JSON/JSON-LD/Markdown, shows a field-by-field parse preview, flags malformed quantities/units and oversized fields, offers explicit repair transforms, and exports a validated neutral recipe bundle. Non-goals: web scraping, generative rewriting, hosted recipe storage, or automatic nutrition calculation.
success_measure: On a corpus of 50 failed samples, the tool explains and repairs at least 70% without a user opening raw JSON.
monetization: free — open local conversion rules build trust and enable format contributions.
constraints: Process files in-browser; preserve attribution/source URLs; do not bypass sites or extract copyrighted recipe content from a URL; make every transformation reversible.
why_distinct: This is a deterministic repair bench for user-owned files, not a thin AI recipe parser.

title: Recipe Library Move Check
user: A household switching between self-hosted recipe apps who needs to know what will be duplicated, lost, or unshareable before importing the family library.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A FoodYou user says they love its privacy but cannot switch without a way to share recipes with family members, and proposes Tandoor import.
A Tandoor user reports a Mealie import failing on a uniqueness constraint, showing that practical cross-library migration remains fragile.

recurrence: Independent June and August 2026 migration requests show that privacy and family sharing choices are blocked by unreliable moves between recipe systems.
current_workaround: Attempt the destination import, accept duplicates/losses, keep both systems running, or manually rebuild a shared library.
incumbents_and_gap: Tandoor, Mealie, FoodYou, and Nextcloud Cookbook have import/export features, but none provides a neutral preflight report for duplicate recipes, missing images, household ownership, and incompatible fields.
smallest_useful_product: Local CLI/desktop checker that reads export folders from two supported systems, creates a proposed neutral inventory, reports collisions and unmapped fields, and writes a reviewable migration checklist. Non-goals: syncing live servers, managing accounts, copying paid content, or acting as a recipe service.
success_measure: For supported exports, 90% of recipe collisions and unmapped fields are identified before the user runs a destination import.
monetization: one-time — migration planning has high but infrequent value.
constraints: Run locally with user-exported data only; do not transfer account credentials; image hashes are metadata, not a license to redistribute content; support explicit data deletion.
why_distinct: It de-risks the decision to move rather than becoming another shared recipe manager.

title: Family Meal Lanes
user: A household planning a week of meals for different people who needs to see who a meal is for, what is shared, and what prep overlaps without signing everyone into a meal service.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Nextcloud Cookbook feature request bundles recipe dimensions, costing, allergens, sub-recipes, and calendar integration—evidence that recipes need planning context.
A KitchenOwl user planning for self, spouse, and family finds multiple meals per day confusing because the planner does not show which person each meal belongs to.

recurrence: Two separate household recipe/planning projects ask for calendar context; the second request names the exact multi-person ambiguity that ordinary weekly grids miss.
current_workaround: Put names in meal titles, maintain separate calendars, message family members, or use multiple overlapping meal plans.
incumbents_and_gap: Mealime, Paprika, Mealie, Tandoor, and KitchenOwl offer meal calendars, but their unit is usually one household dinner, not privacy-preserving lanes for shared and individual meals.
smallest_useful_product: Offline shared-device PWA with a seven-day grid, named local lanes, shared-meal links, prep labels, printable view, and an exportable JSON file. Non-goals: recipes, grocery ordering, nutrition scoring, accounts, or real-time cloud collaboration.
success_measure: In a two-week household trial, planners can answer 'who is this for?' for 95% of scheduled meals without opening a note or asking someone.
monetization: one-time — a kitchen tablet utility should work for a household without a subscription or family account.
constraints: Local-first shared-device data; no child profiling; make printing and manual file transfer first-class; do not make allergen safety claims.
why_distinct: The distinctive primitive is person and shared-meal lanes, not another recipe catalog.

title: Shopping List Handoff
user: A household cook who needs to hand a precise shopping list to someone who does not use the same meal-planning app.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Nextcloud Cookbook user asks for a button that sends recipe ingredients directly to a chosen shopping list.
A KitchenOwl request asks to export a shopping list as text or to another app specifically for someone who does not use KitchenOwl.

recurrence: Two independent 2026 requests make interoperability—not list creation—the pain: the purchaser may be outside the app's household/account boundary.
current_workaround: Screenshots, copied text, SMS messages, paper lists, or persuading every shopper to install the same app.
incumbents_and_gap: AnyList, Google Keep, KitchenOwl, Mealie, and Nextcloud Shopping List support lists but often assume shared accounts or lose recipe quantities/context on handoff.
smallest_useful_product: Static local web page that turns pasted ingredients or a neutral recipe bundle into a concise, unit-normalized, checkable handoff card with print, plain-text, QR, and expiration-free local file options. Non-goals: retailer ordering, user accounts, live collaborative sync, or automatic web recipe extraction.
success_measure: At least 80% of test recipients can complete a list without installing an app, and list creators report fewer than one clarification message per shop.
monetization: free — frictionless sharing matters more than account conversion; optional printable templates could be paid later.
constraints: No cloud storage by default; QR payloads must not expose household addresses or sensitive notes; unit conversion needs clear warnings for ambiguous produce quantities.
why_distinct: It optimizes the handoff boundary between users and apps rather than duplicating a full grocery-list platform.

title: Storage-Aware Expiry
user: A household tracking pantry/freezer stock who needs date defaults and a practical use-first view that change with storage location.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A KitchenOwl user proposes first-class household inventory by fridge, freezer, and pantry with optional quantities, low-stock alerts, and expiry dates.
A Grocy request notes that freezing an item incorrectly defaults to the normal due date and asks for freezer-specific best-before defaults.

recurrence: Two inventory products receive storage-location requests; date handling is wrong or absent precisely where households need it to reduce forgotten food.
current_workaround: Write dates on containers, use a generic reminder, guess after freezing, or buy a heavy self-hosted stock-management system.
incumbents_and_gap: Grocy, KitchenOwl, NoWaste, and Pantry Check track inventory, but a very small location-aware date helper is still missing for users unwilling to inventory every purchase.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA for optional item cards: storage location, frozen-on date, user-configured shelf-life presets, use-first queue, and printable freezer label. Non-goals: barcode catalog, automated purchase tracking, nutrition data, or claims that food is safe to consume.
success_measure: In a six-week pilot, users add at least 15 stored items and mark at least 30% of consumed items from the use-first queue before their chosen date.
monetization: one-time — a low-frequency household utility should not require an ongoing subscription.
constraints: Dates are planning reminders, not food-safety advice; all data local; label printer support only through browser print in v1.
why_distinct: It deliberately avoids full pantry accounting and focuses on the storage/date decision that makes inventory worthwhile.

title: Home Asset Lineage
user: A homeowner documenting appliances, components, and maintenance who needs nested assets to retain their true locations and maintenance history when moved or replaced.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Homebox user reports that parent and child items cannot be stored in different locations, a real limitation for componentized home inventory.
A separate Homebox issue reports duplicating a maintenance item from the global maintenance page fails because its item identity is lost.

recurrence: Two detailed Homebox reports in August 2026 expose the same structural gap: home assets have both a component hierarchy and an independent service/location lifecycle.
current_workaround: Flatten the inventory, duplicate records, put child locations in notes, or keep maintenance in a separate calendar/spreadsheet.
incumbents_and_gap: Homebox, Grocy, Notion, and home-maintenance apps store assets or reminders; they commonly force a single location tree or detach maintenance from the exact component being serviced.
smallest_useful_product: Local-first desktop app for a modest home asset graph: asset, parent asset, actual location, warranty/document links, service events, and an exportable maintenance history. Non-goals: insurance claims submission, contractor marketplace, IoT discovery, or multi-property SaaS.
success_measure: A homeowner can locate any of 20 seeded assets and its latest service event in under 30 seconds, even when it is a component of another asset.
monetization: one-time — durable offline records and document ownership are central to the value proposition.
constraints: Encrypt local document references/attachments at rest where platform support permits; avoid valuation or insurance coverage guarantees; user controls all backups.
why_distinct: It models location and component lineage separately, rather than being another flat home-inventory list.

title: Bank Import Receipts
user: A local-first budgeter importing bank files who needs a trustworthy explanation of what was read, ignored, duplicated, and changed before it affects the budget.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A new Actual user downloads bank transactions, clicks import, sees nothing happen, and must open browser developer tools to investigate.
A Firefly III request asks to extend automatic balance checking into the banking flow, showing that imported balances need explicit verification.

recurrence: Two independent local-first finance projects surface import opacity and balance verification within the same week; this is a trust-breaking failure, not a cosmetic bug.
current_workaround: Retry the import, inspect browser logs, manually compare balances, or postpone using a self-hosted budget tool.
incumbents_and_gap: Actual, Firefly III, YNAB, and bank importers ingest transactions, but errors and balance deltas are often hidden behind an import action rather than delivered as a reviewable receipt.
smallest_useful_product: Local CSV/OFX/QIF preflight tool that detects encoding/date/column errors, previews normalized transactions, estimates duplicates, reconciles opening/closing balance when supplied, and exports a signed import receipt. Non-goals: bank credential aggregation, transaction categorization AI, budgeting, or cloud storage.
success_measure: On a pilot corpus, users diagnose 90% of malformed imports without developer tools and can explain every balance mismatch before importing.
monetization: free — browser-local financial file validation needs maximum trust and no data upload.
constraints: Never transmit or retain financial files; clear all memory on refresh; parser hardening for untrusted CSV/OFX/QIF; do not provide financial advice.
why_distinct: It is an explainable preflight and audit artifact that complements budget apps instead of cloning one.
